3.text: higher than the stature of a man.

4.text: On the large island of Aˊčon, near Chaun Bay, is an ancient mound of

5.text: antlers which is connected with the name of Qeˊeqi, a female shaman whose

6.text: funeral had been held at that place. The mound is said to be very old, and

7.text: is partly sunk into the ground. The part exposed is still more than a fathom

8.text: high and five fathoms in diameter. I saw also in the Anui country heaps

9.text: which, perhaps, had been more than half a century in accumulating, and

10.text: which already contained several hundred sets of antlers.

11.text: In contrast with the commemorative sacrifice, which is almost always

12.text: personal, the “antlers’ store,” as soon as it reaches the proportions of a heap,

13.text: partly loses its personal character, and may commemorate all members of

14.text: the family. Thus, in the funeral places of the Maritime people, where all

15.text: the dead of the village are exposed, the antlers are gathered into several

16.text: large heaps, in commemoration of all the dead whose bodies were disposed

17.text: of near it. New sets of antlers are brought in by individual families for their

18.text: dead, but after a while they are added to one of the common heaps.

19.text: I know of cases among the Reindeer people where whole families were

20.text: swept off by famine or disease, and the relatives, unwilling to leave them

21.text: without funeral, would bring a collective sacrifice for the whole family, and

22.text: then build up an “antlers’ store,” without even caring to find the place where

23.text: the bodies of the dead were lying.

24.text: In some cases a person dying in a strange country, as while on a

25.text: trading-expedition, will express a desire to be laid in his native land. This

26.text: desire may be made known either before the end, or, as happens more

27.text: frequently, afterward, by divination. However, the body of the dead is very

28.text: rarely taken to his home, but is disposed of on the spot. Then, when his

29.text: people return to their own country, they arrange another ceremony, which

30.text: is performed with the same details as if they had the body. Even an

31.text: “enclosure of the dead one” is made of stones or logs, and an “antlers’

32.text: store” is arranged close to it. From that time this place is considered as

33.text: the actual funeral place of the deceased person, and it receives from year to

35.text: FUNERAL, MARITIME CHUKCHEE. — The Maritime people are unable

36.text: to offer sacrifices to the dead in such abundance, and therefore with them

37.text: the whole ceremony is less complicated. The chief features, however, are

38.text: the same. They expose the bodies on the ground, cutting and pulling away

39.text: the clothes, and covering the face and the genitalia with a few strips of skin.

40.text: Sometimes thin flat stones are used for the purpose. The body is surrounded
